text: BCG vaccine dataset metadat package contains 13 randomized trials tuberculosis prevention. escalc() computes log risk ratios yi sampling variances vi. metafor::rma() fits random-effects model. matching Bayesian fit reuses effect-size columns. measure = "RR" tells brma() use default prior distributions log risk ratios. default prior distributions weakly informative provide slight regularization toward zero. summary() reports posterior means, credible intervals, (suppressed ) MCMC convergence diagnostics. Convergence diagnostics included default; chain-level visual diagnostics available via plot_diagnostic_trace(), plot_diagnostic_density(), plot_diagnostic_autocorrelation(). posterior mean log risk ratio close REML estimate metafor package; slight pull toward zero reflects default Normal(0, 1) prior distribution. pooled_effect() returns summary, backtransformed risk-ratio scale via transform = "EXP": plot() visualizes posterior distribution, prior = TRUE overlays prior distribution shift prior posterior visible.
code: data("dat.bcg", package = "metadat")  dat <- metafor::escalc(   ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg,   measure = "RR", data = dat.bcg ) fit1_metafor <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "REML") fit1_metafor #>  #> Random-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: REML) #>  #> tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.3132 (SE = 0.1664) #> tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.5597 #> I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   92.22% #> H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  12.86 #>  #> Test for Heterogeneity: #> Q(df = 12) = 152.2330, p-val < .0001 #>  #> Model Results: #>  #> estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub       #>  -0.7145  0.1798  -3.9744  <.0001  -1.0669  -0.3622  ***  #>  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 fit1_brma <- brma(   yi = yi, vi = vi, measure = "RR",   data = dat, seed = 1 ) summary(fit1_brma, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Random-Effects Model (k = 13) #>  #> Estimates #>       Mean    SD  0.025    0.5  0.975 #> mu  -0.688 0.186 -1.056 -0.682 -0.292 #> tau  0.563 0.136  0.334  0.552  0.858 pooled_effect(fit1_brma, transform = "EXP") #>  #> Pooled Effect Size (risk ratio) #>     Mean Median 0.025 0.975 #> mu 0.511  0.506 0.348 0.747 #> Effect estimates are summarized on the risk ratio scale using EXP on the log risk ratio measure. par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)) plot(fit1_brma, parameter = "mu", prior = TRUE, xlim = c(-3, 3))

title: Bayesian Meta-Analysis
text: continuous moderator can added standard formula syntax via mods argument. ablat absolute latitude trial, frequently used explain BCG effect-size variation. regplot() produces familiar bubble plot fitted regression line.  predict() returns posterior summaries user-specified moderator values.
code: fit2_metafor <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = dat) fit2_metafor #>  #> Mixed-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: REML) #>  #> tau^2 (estimated amount of residual heterogeneity):     0.0764 (SE = 0.0591) #> tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):             0.2763 #> I^2 (residual heterogeneity / unaccounted variability): 68.39% #> H^2 (unaccounted variability / sampling variability):   3.16 #> R^2 (amount of heterogeneity accounted for):            75.62% #>  #> Test for Residual Heterogeneity: #> QE(df = 11) = 30.7331, p-val = 0.0012 #>  #> Test of Moderators (coefficient 2): #> QM(df = 1) = 16.3571, p-val < .0001 #>  #> Model Results: #>  #>          estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub       #> intrcpt    0.2515  0.2491   1.0095  0.3127  -0.2368   0.7397       #> ablat     -0.0291  0.0072  -4.0444  <.0001  -0.0432  -0.0150  ***  #>  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 fit2_brma <- brma(   yi = yi, vi = vi, measure = "RR",   mods = ~ ablat,   data = dat, seed = 1 ) summary(fit2_brma, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Mixed-Effect Model (k = 13) #>  #> Common Estimates #>      Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> tau 0.303 0.131 0.088 0.289 0.587 #>  #> Meta-Regression #>             Mean    SD  0.025    0.5  0.975 #> intercept  0.217 0.275 -0.362  0.237  0.712 #> ablat     -0.028 0.008 -0.043 -0.028 -0.011 par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.8, cex.main = 0.75) metafor::regplot(fit2_metafor, main = "metafor", xlim = c(10, 60), ylim = c(-2, 0.5)) regplot(fit2_brma, main = "RoBMA", xlim = c(10, 60), ylim = c(-2, 0.5)) new_data <- data.frame(ablat = c(15, 35, 55)) predict(fit2_brma, newdata = new_data, type = "terms") #>  #> Location Term Posterior Prediction: #>         Mean Median  0.025  0.975 #> mu[1] -0.196 -0.182 -0.587  0.123 #> mu[2] -0.746 -0.743 -0.994 -0.506 #> mu[3] -1.297 -1.307 -1.722 -0.835

title: Bayesian Meta-Analysis
text: Marginal likelihoods enable model comparison via Bayes factors (Kass & Raftery, 1995). attaching marginal likelihoods fits add_marglik(), bf() returns Bayes factor one model another. Bayes factor quantifies much data shift relative predictive support two models. obtain strong evidence favor model including ablat predictor.
code: fit1_brma <- add_marglik(fit1_brma) fit2_brma <- add_marglik(fit2_brma) bf(fit2_brma, fit1_brma) #> Bayes factor in favor of Model 1 over Model 2: 14.76119

title: Bayesian Meta-Analysis
text: alloc three-level factor describing trial allocation method (random, alternate, systematic). formula syntax extends meta-regression. RoBMA R package also allows direct visualization categorical moderators bubble plot (metafor package supports single dummy coefficient moment).  marginal_means() computes estimated marginal means moderator term, averaging moderators fit. Continuous moderators (ablat) evaluated −1-1, 00, +1+1 standard deviations predictor; categorical moderators (alloc) level. plot() function visualizes posterior distribution estimated marginal means.
code: fit3_metafor <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat + alloc, data = dat) fit3_brma <- brma(   yi = yi, vi = vi, measure = "RR",   mods = ~ ablat + alloc,   data = dat, seed = 1 ) summary(fit3_brma, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Mixed-Effect Model (k = 13) #>  #> Common Estimates #>      Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> tau 0.344 0.144 0.100 0.330 0.674 #>  #> Meta-Regression #>                     Mean    SD  0.025    0.5  0.975 #> intercept          0.287 0.355 -0.468  0.312  0.929 #> ablat             -0.026 0.009 -0.042 -0.027 -0.008 #> alloc[random]     -0.249 0.251 -0.749 -0.248  0.251 #> alloc[systematic]  0.003 0.276 -0.489 -0.017  0.580 par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.8, cex.main = 0.75) metafor::regplot(fit3_metafor, mod = "allocrandom", main = "metafor: random dummy", ylim = c(-2, 0.5)) regplot(fit3_brma, mod = "alloc", main = "RoBMA: alloc factor", ylim = c(-2, 0.5)) emm <- marginal_means(fit3_brma) summary(emm) #>  #> Marginal Means: #>                     Mean    SD  0.025    0.5  0.975 #> intercept         -0.592 0.217 -1.061 -0.585 -0.180 #> ablat[-1SD]       -0.212 0.247 -0.737 -0.197  0.234 #> ablat[0SD]        -0.592 0.217 -1.061 -0.585 -0.180 #> ablat[1SD]        -0.971 0.254 -1.494 -0.971 -0.429 #> alloc[alternate]  -0.592 0.217 -1.061 -0.585 -0.180 #> alloc[random]     -0.841 0.177 -1.192 -0.833 -0.516 #> alloc[systematic] -0.588 0.214 -0.999 -0.605 -0.154 par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1), cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.8, cex.main = 0.75) plot(emm, parameter = "alloc", xlim = c(-2, 0.5), lwd = 2)

title: Multilevel Meta-Analysis
text: school-calendar dataset metadat package contains 56 standardized mean differences nested 11 school districts. Effect sizes yi sampling variances vi already provided, escalc() step needed. metafor::rma.mv() fits multilevel random-effects model compound-symmetric structure random = ~ school | district, parameterized total heterogeneity τ\tau within-district correlation ρ\rho. matching Bayesian fit replaces random = ... argument cluster = district. brma() parameterizes multilevel model compound-symmetric form: total heterogeneity τ\tau cluster-level allocation ρ\rho τbetween=τρ\tau_{} = \tau\sqrt{\rho} τwithin=τ1−ρ\tau_{within} = \tau\sqrt{1 - \rho}. measure = "SMD" selects default prior distributions standardized mean differences. summary() reports posterior means, credible intervals, (suppressed ) MCMC convergence diagnostics mu, tau, rho. posterior mean pooled effect tracks REML estimate metafor package, comparable cluster-level allocation rho total heterogeneity tau.
code: data("dat.konstantopoulos2011", package = "metadat") dat <- dat.konstantopoulos2011 head(dat) #>  #>   district school study year     yi    vi  #> 1       11      1     1 1976 -0.180 0.118  #> 2       11      2     2 1976 -0.220 0.118  #> 3       11      3     3 1976  0.230 0.144  #> 4       11      4     4 1976 -0.300 0.144  #> 5       12      1     5 1989  0.130 0.014  #> 6       12      2     6 1989 -0.260 0.014 fit1_metafor <- metafor::rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ school | district, data = dat) fit1_metafor #>  #> Multivariate Meta-Analysis Model (k = 56; method: REML) #>  #> Variance Components: #>  #> outer factor: district (nlvls = 11) #> inner factor: school   (nlvls = 11) #>  #>             estim    sqrt  fixed  #> tau^2      0.0978  0.3127     no  #> rho        0.6653             no  #>  #> Test for Heterogeneity: #> Q(df = 55) = 578.8640, p-val < .0001 #>  #> Model Results: #>  #> estimate      se    zval    pval   ci.lb   ci.ub     #>   0.1847  0.0846  2.1845  0.0289  0.0190  0.3504  *  #>  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 fit1_brma <- brma(   yi = yi, vi = vi, measure = "SMD",   cluster = district,   data = dat, seed = 1 ) summary(fit1_brma, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Multilevel Random-Effects Model (k = 56, clusters = 11) #>  #> Estimates #>      Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> mu  0.183 0.089 0.009 0.182 0.365 #> tau 0.323 0.058 0.233 0.314 0.461 #> rho 0.634 0.140 0.329 0.647 0.863

title: Publication-Bias Adjustment
text: three model types use separate prior distribution bias-adjustment parameter, independent prior distributions mu, tau, meta-regression coefficients. PET prior distribution invariant effect-size measure. PEESE scale rescaled UISDratio=UISDSMD/UISDmeasure\text{UISD}_{\text{ratio}} = \text{UISD}_{\text{SMD}} / \text{UISD}_{\text{measure}} prior distribution describes comparable bias scale; ratio 11 measure = "SMD". weight-function default specifies Dirichlet prior distribution relative publication probabilities one-sided p-values 0.0250.025, equivalent three-parameter selection model (3PSM). Unlike prior distributions meta-analytic parameters, bias-adjustment prior distributions affected rescale_priors; can replaced via prior_bias, weight-function steps can changed directly via steps argument. bias-adjustment models rely effect_direction argument. Selection models penalize one-sided p-values evaluated expected sign effect, truncated PET PEESE prior distributions constrain small-study coefficient pull estimate toward zero dominant direction. effect_direction argument tells model side . default effect_direction = "detect" infers direction median yi (positive median yields "positive", negative median yields "negative"). Set effect_direction = "positive" effect_direction = "negative" explicitly dominant direction known priori. prior distributions correspond default settings tested larger RoBMA-PSMA ensemble Bartoš et al. (2023). Note three defaults restricted assume presence publication bias: truncated PET / PEESE coefficients constrained pull estimate toward zero, cumulative-Dirichlet weight function forces every non-significant interval’s omega greater -significant interval’s reference value 11. “publication bias” case therefore parameter-space boundary. model-averaged RoBMA() ensemble exactly desired behaviour: separate -bias model carries “selection” hypothesis, bias-adjustment models deliberately one-sided contrast -bias spike sharp inclusion Bayes factor diagnostic. single-model fits vignette companion -bias model ensemble, restriction can shrink estimates toward implied bias even data consistent selection. Flexible Bias Prior Distributions section relaxes restriction model model via prior_bias argument single-model fit analysis interest.

title: Publication-Bias Adjustment
text: PET model regresses effect sizes standard error. metafor::rma() fit passing mods = ~ sqrt(vi); slope sqrt(vi) PET coefficient. RoBMA R package implements PET meta-regression (random-effects heterogeneity component) rather UWLS variant, consistency rest framework. bPET() fits model default Cauchy prior distribution (positive) PET coefficient. measure = "SMD" selects default prior distributions standardized mean differences. posterior mean mu bias-corrected average effect; PET coefficient quantifies strongly small studies pull meta-analytic mean. left panel shows prior posterior PET coefficient prior = TRUE overlaying prior distribution; right panel shows implied PET regression effect standard error plot_pet_peese(), prior band overlaid.  half-Cauchy prior distribution PET wide; posterior concentrates near 11, broadly consistent metafor package estimate pulled toward zero prior distribution. implied regression line intersects distribution effect sizes standard errors.
code: fit_PET_metafor <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ sqrt(vi), data = dat) fit_PET_metafor #>  #> Mixed-Effects Model (k = 81; tau^2 estimator: REML) #>  #> tau^2 (estimated amount of residual heterogeneity):     0.0940 (SE = 0.0236) #> tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):             0.3065 #> I^2 (residual heterogeneity / unaccounted variability): 79.74% #> H^2 (unaccounted variability / sampling variability):   4.94 #> R^2 (amount of heterogeneity accounted for):            8.96% #>  #> Test for Residual Heterogeneity: #> QE(df = 79) = 234.7716, p-val < .0001 #>  #> Test of Moderators (coefficient 2): #> QM(df = 1) = 6.5617, p-val = 0.0104 #>  #> Model Results: #>  #>           estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb   ci.ub     #> intrcpt    -0.0359  0.1038  -0.3455  0.7297  -0.2394  0.1676     #> sqrt(vi)    1.0765  0.4203   2.5616  0.0104   0.2528  1.9002  *  #>  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 fit_PET_brma <- bPET(   yi = yi, vi = vi, measure = "SMD",   data = dat, seed = 1 ) summary(fit_PET_brma, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Random-Effects PET Model (k = 81) #>  #> Estimates #>       Mean    SD  0.025    0.5 0.975 #> mu  -0.004 0.097 -0.196 -0.002 0.181 #> tau  0.307 0.040  0.233  0.305 0.391 #>  #> Publication Bias #>      Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> PET 0.932 0.386 0.214 0.924 1.699 par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.8, cex.main = 0.75) plot(fit_PET_brma,  parameter = "PET", prior = TRUE, main = "PET coefficient", xlim = c(0, 4)) plot_pet_peese(fit_PET_brma, prior = TRUE, main = "PET regression")

title: Publication-Bias Adjustment
text: PEESE model regresses effect sizes sampling variance instead standard error. metafor::rma() fit passing mods = ~ vi; slope vi PEESE coefficient. PET, RoBMA R package PEESE meta-regression version (retaining heterogeneity component), UWLS variant. bPEESE() fits model default Cauchy prior distribution (positive) PEESE coefficient, prior scale rescaled effect-size measure. PET, left panel shows prior posterior PEESE coefficient right panel shows implied PEESE regression effect sampling variance.  bias-corrected effect PEESE also closer zero random-effects estimate due weakly informative prior distributions.
code: fit_PEESE_metafor <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ vi, data = dat) fit_PEESE_metafor #>  #> Mixed-Effects Model (k = 81; tau^2 estimator: REML) #>  #> tau^2 (estimated amount of residual heterogeneity):     0.0917 (SE = 0.0232) #> tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):             0.3028 #> I^2 (residual heterogeneity / unaccounted variability): 79.77% #> H^2 (unaccounted variability / sampling variability):   4.94 #> R^2 (amount of heterogeneity accounted for):            11.18% #>  #> Test for Residual Heterogeneity: #> QE(df = 79) = 231.8504, p-val < .0001 #>  #> Test of Moderators (coefficient 2): #> QM(df = 1) = 5.6925, p-val = 0.0170 #>  #> Model Results: #>  #>          estimate      se    zval    pval    ci.lb   ci.ub     #> intrcpt    0.0903  0.0647  1.3959  0.1627  -0.0365  0.2171     #> vi         1.8824  0.7890  2.3859  0.0170   0.3360  3.4287  *  #>  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 fit_PEESE_brma <- bPEESE(   yi = yi, vi = vi, measure = "SMD",   data = dat, seed = 1 ) summary(fit_PEESE_brma, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Random-Effects PEESE Model (k = 81) #>  #> Estimates #>      Mean    SD  0.025   0.5 0.975 #> mu  0.092 0.063 -0.031 0.092 0.216 #> tau 0.304 0.041  0.230 0.302 0.389 #>  #> Publication Bias #>        Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> PEESE 1.840 0.759 0.376 1.837 3.350 par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.8, cex.main = 0.75) plot(fit_PEESE_brma, parameter = "PEESE", prior = TRUE, main = "PEESE coefficient", xlim = c(0, 8)) plot_pet_peese(fit_PEESE_brma, prior = TRUE, main = "PEESE regression")

title: Publication-Bias Adjustment
text: selection model multiplies likelihood study p-value-dependent publication probability. metafor package, one-sided three-parameter model fit passing random-effects fit metafor::selmodel(). bselmodel() fits model one call. default weight function uses single one-sided cutoff 0.0250.025. Passing steps = c(0.025, 0.5) (vector) specifies finer step function; prior distribution omega vector uniform across implied intervals. default Dirichlet prior distribution omega RoBMA R package enforces monotonically decreasing weight function (non-significant intervals exceed reference interval), matches metafor::selmodel(..., decreasing = TRUE) . omega vector reported omega[0, 0.025] fixed 11 reference interval; omega[0.025, 1] publication probability one-sided p-values 0.0250.025 relative significant interval. Values 11 indicate non-significant studies reported less often significant ones. omega vector one panel per interval (reference [0,0.025][0, 0.025] panel shows spike 11). plot_weightfunction() visualizes weights step function one-sided p-value scale, prior band overlaid.   bias-corrected mu posterior shifted toward zero relative brma() random-effects fit, magnitude shift driven gap prior posterior omega[0.025, 1].
code: fit_rma_metafor      <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "ML") fit_selmodel_metafor <- metafor::selmodel(fit_rma_metafor, type = "stepfun", steps = .025, decreasing = TRUE) fit_selmodel_metafor #>  #> Random-Effects Model (k = 81; tau^2 estimator: ML) #>  #> tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.0811 (SE = 0.0261) #> tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.2848 #>  #> Test for Heterogeneity: #> LRT(df = 1) = 37.3674, p-val < .0001 #>  #> Model Results: #>  #> estimate      se    zval    pval   ci.lb   ci.ub     #>   0.1328  0.0655  2.0267  0.0427  0.0044  0.2612  *  #>  #> Test for Selection Model Parameters: #> LRT(df = 1) = 1.7646, p-val = 0.1840 #>  #> Selection Model Results: #>  #>                      k  estimate      se     zval    pval   ci.lb   ci.ub     #> 0     < p <= 0.025  25    1.0000     ---      ---     ---     ---     ---     #> 0.025 < p <= 1      56    0.5485  0.2495  -1.8097  0.0703  0.0594  1.0000  .  #>  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 fit_selmodel_brma <- bselmodel(   yi = yi, vi = vi, measure = "SMD",   data = dat, seed = 1 ) summary(fit_selmodel_brma, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Random-Effects Selection Model (k = 81) #>  #> Estimates #>      Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> mu  0.141 0.057 0.029 0.142 0.252 #> tau 0.293 0.043 0.212 0.292 0.380 #>  #> Publication Bias #>                 Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> omega[0,0.025] 1.000 0.000 1.000 1.000 1.000 #> omega[0.025,1] 0.621 0.192 0.273 0.614 0.969 #> P-value intervals for publication bias weights omega correspond to one-sided p-values. par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.8, cex.main = 0.75) plot(fit_selmodel_brma, parameter = "omega", prior = TRUE, xlim = c(0, 1)) par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.8, cex.main = 0.75) plot_weightfunction(fit_selmodel_brma, prior = TRUE, main = "Weight-function")

title: Publication-Bias Adjustment
text: PET natural relaxation drop [0, Inf] truncation bias coefficient. keep default Cauchy family scale (Cauchy(0, 1)) comparison isolates effect removing lower bound; prior distribution now puts equal mass negative-bias regions, small studies pull estimate rather . two panels show prior posterior PET coefficient default truncated prior distribution (left) relaxed full-real-line prior distribution (right). dashed line PET = 0 marks default prior distribution bounded relaxed prior distribution places mass sides.
code: fit_PET_brma_flex <- bPET(   yi = yi, vi = vi, measure = "SMD",   prior_bias = prior_PET(     distribution = "cauchy",     parameters = list(location = 0, scale = 1),     truncation = list(lower = -Inf, upper = Inf)   ),   data = dat, seed = 1 ) summary(fit_PET_brma_flex, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Random-Effects PET Model (k = 81) #>  #> Estimates #>       Mean    SD  0.025    0.5 0.975 #> mu  -0.004 0.102 -0.207 -0.004 0.191 #> tau  0.308 0.040  0.234  0.305 0.391 #>  #> Publication Bias #>      Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> PET 0.933 0.408 0.167 0.929 1.755 par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.8, cex.main = 0.85) plot(fit_PET_brma,      parameter = "PET", prior = TRUE,   main = "PET (default)",     xlim = c(-2, 4)) abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50") plot(fit_PET_brma_flex, parameter = "PET", prior = TRUE,   main = "PET (untruncated)", xlim = c(-2, 4)) abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")

title: Location-Scale Meta-Analysis
text: writing--learn dataset contains 48 standardized mean differences studies effectiveness school-based writing interventions academic achievement. Effect sizes yi sampling variances vi already provided. start standard random-effects model scale predictor. pooled effect single heterogeneity parameter tau track REML estimates metafor package.
code: data("dat.bangertdrowns2004", package = "metadat") dat <- dat.bangertdrowns2004 dat$ni100 <- dat$ni / 100 dat$meta  <- as.factor(dat$meta) dat$imag  <- as.factor(dat$imag) fit1_metafor <- metafor::rma(yi, vi, data = dat) fit1_metafor #>  #> Random-Effects Model (k = 48; tau^2 estimator: REML) #>  #> tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.0499 (SE = 0.0197) #> tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.2235 #> I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   58.37% #> H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  2.40 #>  #> Test for Heterogeneity: #> Q(df = 47) = 107.1061, p-val < .0001 #>  #> Model Results: #>  #> estimate      se    zval    pval   ci.lb   ci.ub       #>   0.2219  0.0460  4.8209  <.0001  0.1317  0.3122  ***  #>  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 fit1_brma <- brma(   yi = yi, vi = vi, measure = "SMD",   data = dat, seed = 1 ) summary(fit1_brma, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Random-Effects Model (k = 48) #>  #> Estimates #>      Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> mu  0.220 0.048 0.130 0.220 0.317 #> tau 0.227 0.053 0.131 0.224 0.340

title: Location-Scale Meta-Analysis
text: Sample size natural candidate explaining heterogeneity: smaller studies often produce variable estimates larger ones. add rescaled total sample size (ni100 = ni / 100) location scale side. location coefficient ni100 matches REML estimate metafor package. scale block reports exp(intercept), baseline -study heterogeneity τ\tau, multiplicative log-scale coefficient ni100. Note metafor::rma() regresses log(τ2)\log(\tau^2) brma() regresses log(τ)\log(\tau), metafor package scale coefficient exactly twice matching brma() coefficient. regplot() pi = TRUE overlays prediction interval bubble plot. τ\tau varies ni100, brma() prediction band narrows toward larger sample sizes, model expects less -study heterogeneity. metafor::regplot() currently draw prediction interval location-scale models, regression line confidence band appear left panel.
code: fit2_metafor <- suppressWarnings(metafor::rma(   yi, vi,   mods  = ~ ni100,   scale = ~ ni100,   data = dat )) fit2_metafor #>  #> Location-Scale Model (k = 48; tau^2 estimator: REML) #>  #> Test for Residual Heterogeneity: #> QE(df = 46) = 95.1352, p-val < .0001 #>  #> Test of Location Coefficients (coefficient 2): #> QM(df = 1) = 7.8268, p-val = 0.0051 #>  #> Model Results (Location): #>  #>          estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub       #> intrcpt    0.3017  0.0661   4.5629  <.0001   0.1721   0.4313  ***  #> ni100     -0.0553  0.0198  -2.7976  0.0051  -0.0940  -0.0165   **  #>  #> Test of Scale Coefficients (coefficient 2): #> QM(df = 1) = 3.1850, p-val = 0.0743 #>  #> Model Results (Scale): #>  #>          estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub      #> intrcpt   -1.9209  0.6690  -2.8713  0.0041  -3.2321  -0.6097  **  #> ni100     -0.9174  0.5141  -1.7847  0.0743  -1.9250   0.0901   .  #>  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 fit2_brma <- brma(   yi = yi, vi = vi, measure = "SMD",   mods  = ~ ni100,   scale = ~ ni100,   data = dat, seed = 1 ) summary(fit2_brma, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Location-Scale Model (k = 48) #>  #> Location #>             Mean    SD  0.025    0.5  0.975 #> intercept  0.303 0.068  0.171  0.302  0.437 #> ni100     -0.056 0.023 -0.103 -0.056 -0.013 #>  #> Scale #>                  Mean    SD  0.025    0.5 0.975 #> exp(intercept)  0.348 0.118  0.148  0.338 0.608 #> ni100          -0.375 0.225 -0.865 -0.366 0.042 #> exp(Intercept) corresponds to the between-study heterogeneity tau; the meta-regression coefficients correspond to the multiplicative effects on log-scale. par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.8, cex.main = 0.75) metafor::regplot(fit2_metafor, mod = "ni100", pi = TRUE,                  main = "metafor", xlim = c(0, 6), ylim = c(-1, 2)) regplot(fit2_brma, mod = "ni100", pi = TRUE,         main = "RoBMA",   xlim = c(0, 6), ylim = c(-1, 2))

title: Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Meta-Analysis
text: BCG vaccine dataset metadat package contains 13 randomized trials tuberculosis prevention. Treated control event counts (tpos, tneg, cpos, cneg) passed directly. metafor::rma.glmm() fits random-effects logistic model. use model = "UM.FS" obtain unconditional model fixed study-specific intercepts, formulation corresponds binomial GLMM brma.glmm() (Model 4 Jackson et al. (2018)). matching Bayesian fit takes count columns measure = "". summary() reports posterior means, credible intervals, (suppressed ) MCMC convergence diagnostics pooled log odds ratio mu heterogeneity tau. posterior mean mu tracks maximum-likelihood estimate metafor package, comparable heterogeneity tau. pooled_effect() returns summary backtransformed odds-ratio scale via transform = "EXP":
code: data("dat.bcg", package = "metadat") head(dat.bcg) #>   trial               author year tpos  tneg cpos  cneg ablat     alloc #> 1     1              Aronson 1948    4   119   11   128    44    random #> 2     2     Ferguson & Simes 1949    6   300   29   274    55    random #> 3     3      Rosenthal et al 1960    3   228   11   209    42    random #> 4     4    Hart & Sutherland 1977   62 13536  248 12619    52    random #> 5     5 Frimodt-Moller et al 1973   33  5036   47  5761    13 alternate #> 6     6      Stein & Aronson 1953  180  1361  372  1079    44 alternate fit1_metafor <- metafor::rma.glmm(   ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg, measure = "OR",    model = "UM.FS", data = dat.bcg ) fit1_metafor #>  #> Random-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: ML) #> Model Type: Unconditional Model with Fixed Study Effects #>  #> tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.2949 #> tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.5430 #> I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   91.02% #> H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  11.14 #>  #> Tests for Heterogeneity: #> Wld(df = 12) = 163.1649, p-val < .0001 #> LRT(df = 12) = 176.9544, p-val < .0001 #>  #> Model Results: #>  #> estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub       #>  -0.7450  0.1756  -4.2434  <.0001  -1.0891  -0.4009  ***  #>  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 fit1_brma <- brma.glmm(   ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg, measure = "OR",   data = dat.bcg, seed = 1 ) summary(fit1_brma, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Random-Effects Model (k = 13) #>  #> Estimates #>       Mean    SD  0.025    0.5  0.975 #> mu  -0.719 0.183 -1.089 -0.718 -0.353 #> tau  0.589 0.141  0.361  0.569  0.922 pooled_effect(fit1_brma, transform = "EXP") #>  #> Pooled Effect Size (odds ratio) #>     Mean Median 0.025 0.975 #> mu 0.495  0.488 0.337 0.703 #> Effect estimates are summarized on the odds ratio scale using EXP on the log odds ratio measure.

what: Default Prior Distributions and the Auxiliary Parameter
title: Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Meta-Analysis
text: default prior distributions mu tau follow unit-information set-elsewhere package, scaled known unit information standard deviation chosen measure (sqrt(4) IRR). Beyond mu tau, GLMM models include estimate-specific nuisance parameters per-study baseline level. binomial outcomes (measure = ""), logit(pi[]) midpoint two arm logits applying half study-specific log odds ratio arm. default prior_baserate = Beta(1, 1) placed independently pi[]. Poisson outcomes (measure = "IRR"), phi[] midpoint two arm log incidence rates applying half study-specific log incidence rate ratio arm. midpoint log-rate unbounded, bounded flat default analogous Beta(1, 1), default prior_lograte proper data-based unit-information normal used independently phi[]. Thus default nuisance-parameter prior distributions exchangeable iid sense, hierarchical prior distributions learned common baseline-rate distribution. defaults can overridden via corresponding prior_* argument; see Prior Distributions vignette. Poisson model corresponds Bagos & Nikolopoulos (2009) uses event counts exposure times (x1i, t1i, x2i, t2i) place four-way count layout.

title: Bayesian Model Averaging
text: metafor::rma.uni() fits conventional random-effects model standardized mean differences. Bayesian counterpart uses brma() default prior distributions: Normal(0, 0.71) unit-information prior distribution effect Normal(0, 0.35)[0, Inf] half-normal prior distribution heterogeneity. Setting heterogeneity prior distribution spike zero turns random-effects model fixed-effect model. marginal likelihoods attached models via add_marglik(), bf() returns Bayes factor two fits. Bayes factor close one neither model decisively preferred. Rather picking one two models, can model-average weight inference posterior model probabilities.
code: res <- metafor::rma.uni(   yi = smd, sei = se,   data = dat, method = "REML" ) res #>  #> Random-Effects Model (k = 23; tau^2 estimator: REML) #>  #> tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.0205 (SE = 0.0264) #> tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.1431 #> I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   22.44% #> H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  1.29 #>  #> Test for Heterogeneity: #> Q(df = 22) = 27.5518, p-val = 0.1910 #>  #> Model Results: #>  #> estimate      se    zval    pval   ci.lb   ci.ub       #>   0.5600  0.0652  8.5930  <.0001  0.4322  0.6877  ***  #>  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 fit_RE <- brma(   yi = smd, sei = se, measure = "SMD",   data = dat, seed = 1 ) fit_RE <- add_marglik(fit_RE) summary(fit_RE, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Random-Effects Model (k = 23) #>  #> Estimates #>      Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> mu  0.554 0.070 0.424 0.551 0.701 #> tau 0.140 0.084 0.008 0.134 0.318 fit_FE <- brma(   yi = smd, sei = se, measure = "SMD",   prior_heterogeneity = prior("spike", list(location = 0)),   data = dat, seed = 1 ) fit_FE <- add_marglik(fit_FE) summary(fit_FE, include_mcmc_diagnostics = FALSE) #>  #> Bayesian Random-Effects Model (k = 23) #>  #> Estimates #>     Mean    SD 0.025   0.5 0.975 #> mu 0.525 0.055 0.418 0.525 0.633 bf(fit_RE, fit_FE) #> Bayes factor in favor of Model 1 over Model 2: 0.76191

what: From Two Fits to Model Averaging
title: Bayesian Model Averaging
text: BMA() fits mixture two models one call. top-level prior-distribution argument paired _null version; supply , model averages component. Setting prior_effect_null = NULL drops null component effect (spike zero) leaves 2-model average presence vs absence heterogeneity, BMA analogue comparison . Components table reports posterior probability inclusion Bayes factor heterogeneity. BF closely matches bf(fit_RE, fit_FE) MCMC noise. two routes compute quantity differently: bf() bridge-samples marginal likelihoods two separate fits, BMA() runs single MCMC joint model space model indicator latent variable recovers posterior model probabilities indicator frequencies (Lodewyckx et al., 2011). Adding third fourth component product-space sampler costs one indicator instead set full model fits bridge-sampling runs, makes larger ensembles RoBMA() tractable.

title: Bayesian Model Averaging
text: Bayesian model-averaged meta-analysis, every component paired _null argument (.e. prior_effect prior_effect_null). Either side can NULL (remove component), single prior distribution, list prior distributions (sub-mixture). Common customizations tightening widening slab, replacing point-zero null region practical equivalence, forcing moderator every model. examples use only_priors = TRUE print prior structure without fitting models. Tighten effect slab rescale_priors = 0.5: Replace point-zero null effect small spread around zero (perinull) test region practical equivalence: Force tailor every model dropping null: tighter half-normal slab τ\tau: Empirical informed prior distributions based Cochrane database available via prior_informed_field prior_informed_subfield; see Informed Bayesian Model-Averaged Meta-Analysis Medicine.
code: fit_priors <- BMA(   yi = smd, sei = se, measure = "SMD",   rescale_priors = 0.5,   data = dat, only_priors = TRUE ) print_prior(fit_priors, parameter = "mu") #> mu: #>   alternative: #>     (1/2) * Normal(0, 0.35) #>   null: #>     (1/2) * Spike(0) fit_priors <- BMA(   yi = smd, sei = se, measure = "SMD",   prior_effect_null = prior("normal", list(mean = 0, sd = 0.05)),   data = dat, only_priors = TRUE ) print_prior(fit_priors, parameter = "mu") #> mu: #>   alternative: #>     (1/2) * Normal(0, 0.71) #>   null: #>     (1/2) * Normal(0, 0.05) fit_priors <- BMA(   yi = smd, sei = se, measure = "SMD",   mods = ~ tailor,   prior_mods_null = list(tailor = NULL),   data = dat, only_priors = TRUE ) print_prior(fit_priors, parameter_mods = "tailor") #> mu_tailor: #>   alternative: #>     (1/1) * mean difference contrast: mNormal(0, 0.35) fit_priors <- BMA(   yi = smd, sei = se, measure = "SMD",   prior_heterogeneity = prior(     distribution = "normal",     parameters   = list(mean = 0, sd = 0.25),     truncation   = list(lower = 0)   ),   data = dat, only_priors = TRUE ) print_prior(fit_priors, parameter = "tau") #> tau: #>   alternative: #>     (1/2) * Normal(0, 0.25)[0, Inf] #>   null: #>     (1/2) * Spike(0)

text: second publication bias adjustment perform selection models. Selection models adjust different publication probabilities different p-value intervals. Selection models implemented weightr package (weightfunct() function; Coburn et al. (2019)) newly also metafor package (selmodel() function; Viechtbauer (2010)). First, use weightr implementation fit “4PSM” selection model specifies three distinct p-value intervals: (1) covering range significant p-values effect sizes expected direction (0.00-0.025), (2) covering range “marginally” significant p-values effect sizes expected direction (0.025-0.05), (3) covering range non-significant p-values (0.05-1). use Fisher’s z effect sizes dfz. fit model, need pass effect sizes (dfz$yi) effect argument variances (dfz$vi) v argument (note need pass vector values directly since weightfunct() function allow us pass data frame directly previous functions). set steps = c(0.025, 0.05) specify appropriate cut-points (note steps correspond one-sided p-values), set table = TRUE obtain frequency p values specified intervals. Note warning message informing us fact data contain sufficient number p-values one p-value intervals. model output obtained printing fitted model object fit_4PSM shows one p-value (0.025, 0.05) interval. can deal issue joining “marginally” significant non-significant p-value interval, resulting “3PSM” model. new model suffer estimation problem due limited number p-values intervals, can now interpret results confidence. First, check test heterogeneity clearly rejects null hypothesis Q(df = 17) = 75.4999, $p$ = 5.188348e-09 (find evidence heterogeneity, proceeded fitting fixed-effect version model specifying fe = TRUE argument). follow checking test publication bias likelihood ratio test comparing unadjusted adjusted estimate X^2(df = 1) = 3.107176, $p$ = 0.077948. result test slightly ambiguous: reject null hypothesis publication bias α=0.10\alpha = 0.10 α=0.05\alpha = 0.05. decide interpret estimated effect size, transform back correlation scale. effect size estimate corresponds second value fit_3PSM$adj_est object random effect model. Alternatively, conducted analysis analogously metafor package. use random effect meta-analysis object specify type = "stepfun" argument obtain step weight function set appropriate steps steps = c(0.025) argument. output verifies results obtained previous analysis.
code: fit_4PSM <- weightr::weightfunct(   effect = dfz$yi, v = dfz$vi,   steps = c(0.025, 0.05), table = TRUE ) fit_4PSM #>  #> Unadjusted Model (k = 18): #>  #> tau^2 (estimated amount of total title: Tutorial: Adjusting for Publication Bias in JASP and R - Selection Models, PET-PEESE, and Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis
text: third final publication bias adjustment perform robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA). RoBMA uses Bayesian model-averaging combine inference PET-PEESE selection models. use RoBMA R package (RoBMA() function; Bartoš & Maier (2020)) fit 36-model ensemble based orthogonal combination models assuming presence absence effect size, heterogeneity, publication bias. models assuming presence publication bias split six weight function models models utilizing PET PEESE publication bias adjustment. fit model, pass Fisher’s z effect sizes sampling variances yi vi arguments set measure = "ZCOR". use seed argument make analysis reproducible (uses MCMC sampling, contrast previous methods). turn parallel estimation setting parallel = TRUE argument; parallel processing fails, try rerunning model turning parallel processing . default prior distributions estimation algorithm changed version 3.6.1, specify prior distributions explicitly. prior distributions reproduce version 3.6.1 specification old approximate Cohen’s d Fisher’s z prior rescaling. Cohen’s d scale, effect prior Normal(0, 1), heterogeneity prior InvGamma(1, 0.15), PEESE prior scale 5. step used take time depending CPU. 4.0 version package uses product-space parameterization, notably speeds sampling usually takes minute moderately large datasets. use summary() function explore details fitted model. printed output consists three parts. first table called Component Inclusion contains information fitted models. second column summarizes prior model probabilities models assuming presence individual components. third column contains information posterior probability models assuming presence components; can observe posterior model probabilities models assuming presence effect slightly increased. last column contains information evidence favor presence components. Evidence presence effect undecided; models assuming presence effect ~1.2 times likely given data models assuming absence effect. However, find overwhelming evidence favor heterogeneity, models assuming presence heterogeneity 10,000 times likely given data models assuming absence heterogeneity, moderate evidence favor publication bias. second table called Estimates contains information model-averaged estimates. first row labeled mu corresponds model-averaged effect size estimate Fisher’s z scale second row labeled tau corresponds model-averaged heterogeneity estimates. estimated model-averaged weights different p-value intervals PET PEESE regression coefficients. obtain effect size estimate correlation scale pooled_effect(). Now, obtained model-averaged effect size estimate correlation scale. interested estimates model-averaged across models assuming presence effect, heterogeneity, publication bias, add conditional = TRUE argument summary() function. can also obtain summary information individual models summary_models(). resulting table shows prior posterior model probabilities inclusion Bayes factors individual models. MCMC diagnostics included summary output. Visual diagnostics can requested plot_diagnostic_trace(), plot_diagnostic_density(), plot_diagnostic_autocorrelation().  Finally, can also plot model-averaged posterior distribution plot() function. set prior = TRUE argument include prior distribution grey line (arrow point density zero) output_measure = "COR" transform posterior distribution correlation scale. (par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 4)) call increases left margin figure, secondary y-axis text cut .)

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Model-Averaged Meta-Analysis
text: specify simple hierarchical meta-analytic model (see Konstantopoulos (2011) example). Using distributional notation, can describe data generating process multi-stage sampling procedure. nutshell, assume existence overall mean effect μ\mu. Next, assume effect sizes district k=1,…,Kk = 1, \dots, K, γk\gamma_k, systematically differ mean effect, variance district-level effects summarized heterogeneity τb\tau_{b} (). Furthermore, assume true effects θk,j\theta_{k,j} study j=1,…Jkj = 1, \dots J_k systematically differ district-level effect, variance study effects district-level effect summarized heterogeneity τw\tau_{w} (within). Finally, observed effect sizes yk,jy_{k,j} differ true effects yk,jy_{k,j} due random errors sek,j\text{se}_{k,j}. Mathematically, can describe model : γk∼N(μ,τb2),θk,j∼N(γk,τw2),yk,j∼N(θk,j,sek,j). \begin{aligned}   \gamma_k     &\sim \text{N}(\mu,          \tau_b^2),\\   \theta_{k,j} &\sim \text{N}(\gamma_k,     \tau_w^2),\\    y_{k,j}     &\sim \text{N}(\theta_{k,j}, \text{se}_{k,j}).\\ \end{aligned}  N() denotes normal distribution mean variance. Conveniently, bit algebra, need estimate district-level true study effects. Instead, marginalize , sample observed effect sizes district yk,.y_{k,.} directly multivariate normal distributions, MN(), common mean μ\mu covariance matrix S: yk,.∼MN(μ,S),S=[τb2+τw2+se12τw2…τw2τw2τb2+τw2+se22…τw2…………τw2τw2…τb2+τw2+seJk2]. \begin{aligned}    y_{k,.}  &\sim \text{MN}(\mu, \text{S}),\\    \text{S} &= \begin{bmatrix}        \tau_b^2 + \tau_w^2 + \text{se}_1^2 & \tau_w^2 & \dots & \tau_w^2  \\       \tau_w^2 & \tau_b^2 + \tau_w^2 + \text{se}_2^2 & \dots & \tau_w^2  \\       \dots  & \dots & \dots & \dots \\       \tau_w^2 & \tau_w^2 & \dots & \tau_b^2 + \tau_w^2 + \text{se}_{J_k}^2 & \\   \end{bmatrix}. \end{aligned}  random effects marginalization helpful allows us sample fewer parameters posterior distribution (significantly simplifies marginal likelihood estimation via bridge sampling). Furthermore, marginalization allows us properly specify selection model publication bias adjustment models – marginalization propagates selection process sampling steps (proceed sequential sampling selection procedure observed effect sizes modifies sampling distributions preceding levels). can re-parameterize model performing following substitution, τ2=τb2+τw2,ρ=τw2τb2+τw2, \begin{aligned}    \tau^2 &= \tau_b^2 + \tau_w^2,\\    \rho   &= \frac{\tau_w^2}{\tau_b^2 + \tau_w^2}, \end{aligned}  specifying covariance matrix using inter-study correlation ρ\rho, total heterogeneity τ\tau, standard errors se.\text{se}_{.}: S=[τ2+se12ρτ2…ρτ2ρτ2τ2+se22…ρτ2…………ρτ2ρτ2…τ2+seJk2]. \begin{aligned}    \text{S} &= \begin{bmatrix}        \tau^2 + \text{se}_1^2 & \rho\tau^2 & \dots & \rho\tau^2  \\       \rho\tau^2 & \tau^2 + \text{se}_2^2 & \dots & \rho\tau^2  \\       \dots  & \dots & \dots & \dots \\       \rho\tau^2 & \rho\tau^2 & \dots & \tau^2 + \text{se}_{J_k}^2 & \\   \end{bmatrix}. \end{aligned}  specification corresponds compound symmetry covariance matrix random effects, default settings metafor::rma.mv() function. importantly, allows us easily specify prior distributions correlation coefficient ρ\rho total heterogeneity τ\tau.

title: Reproducing Bayesian Model-Averaged Meta-Analysis
text: illustrate fit classical BMA (adjusting publication bias) using RoBMA. purpose, reproduce meta-analysis registered reports Power posing Gronau et al. (2017). focus analysis reported results using Cauchy prior distribution scale 1/21/\sqrt{2} effect size estimation (half-Cauchy testing) inverse-gamma distribution shape = 1 scale = 0.15 heterogeneity parameter. can find figure original publication paper’s supplementary materials https://osf.io/fxg32/. First, load power posing data provided within metaBMA package reproduce analysis performed Gronau et al. (2017). output, can see inclusion Bayes factor effect size BF10=33.14BF_{10} = 33.14 effect size estimate 0.22, 95% HDI [0.09, 0.34], matches reported results. Please note metaBMA package model-averages across H1H_{1} models, whereas RoBMA package model-averages across models (assuming presence absence effect).
code: data("power_pose", package = "metaBMA") power_pose[,c("study", "effectSize", "SE")] #>                study effectSize        SE #> 1      Bailey et al.  0.2507640 0.2071399 #> 2       Ronay et al.  0.2275180 0.1931046 #> 3 Klaschinski et al.  0.3186069 0.1423228 #> 4     Bombari et al.  0.2832082 0.1421356 #> 5        Latu et al.  0.1463949 0.1416107 #> 6      Keller et al.  0.1509773 0.1221166 fit_BMA_test <- metaBMA::meta_bma(y   = power_pose$effectSize, SE = power_pose$SE,                                   d   = metaBMA::prior(family = "halfcauchy", param = 1/sqrt(2)),                                   tau = metaBMA::prior(family = "invgamma", param = c(1, .15)))   fit_BMA_est  <- metaBMA::meta_bma(y   = power_pose$effectSize, SE = power_pose$SE,                                   d   = metaBMA::prior(family = "cauchy", param = c(0, 1/sqrt(2))),                                   tau = metaBMA::prior(family = "invgamma", param = c(1, .15))) fit_BMA_test$inclusion #> ### Inclusion Bayes factor ### #>       Model Prior Posterior included #> 1  fixed_H0  0.25   0.00868          #> 2  fixed_H1  0.25   0.77745        x #> 3 random_H0  0.25   0.02061          #> 4 random_H1  0.25   0.19325        x #>  #>   Inclusion posterior probability: 0.971  #>   Inclusion Bayes factor: 33.136  round(fit_BMA_est$estimates,2) #>          mean   sd 2.5%  50% 97.5% hpd95_lower hpd95_upper  n_eff Rhat #> averaged 0.22 0.06 0.09 0.22  0.34        0.09        0.34     NA   NA #> fixed    0.22 0.06 0.10 0.22  0.34        0.10        0.34 3026.5    1 #> random   0.22 0.08 0.07 0.22  0.37        0.07        0.37 6600.4    1

title: Reproducing Bayesian Model-Averaged Meta-Analysis
text: Now reproduce analysis RoBMA. set corresponding prior distributions effect sizes (μ\mu) heterogeneity (τ\tau), remove alternative prior distributions publication bias setting priors_bias = NULL. specify half-Cauchy prior distribution RoBMA::prior() function use regular Cauchy distribution truncate zero (note metaBMA RoBMA export prior() functions clash loading packages simultaneously). inverse-gamma prior distribution heterogeneity parameter default option (specify completeness). omit specifications null prior distributions effect size, heterogeneity (set spike 0 default), publication bias (set publication bias default). Note starting version 3.1, package includes NoBMA() function, allows users skip publication bias adjustment directly. Since metaBMA model-averages effect size estimates across models assuming presence effect, remove models assuming absence effect estimation ensemble priors_effect_null = NULL. Finally, set transformation = "cohens_d" estimate models Cohen’s d scale. RoBMA uses Fisher’s z scale default transforms estimated coefficients back scale used specifying prior distributions. speed computation setting parallel = TRUE, set seed reproducibility. output summary.RoBMA() function 2 parts. first one “Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis” heading provides basic summary fitted models component types (presence Effect Heterogeneity). table summarizes prior posterior probabilities inclusion Bayes factors individual components. results half-Cauchy model specified testing show inclusion BF nearly identical one computed metaBMA package, BF10=33.11\text{BF}_{10} = 33.11. second part ‘Model-averaged estimates’ heading displays parameter estimates. results unrestricted Cauchy model specified estimation show effect size estimate μ=0.22\mu = 0.22, 95% CI [0.10, 0.35] also mirrors one obtained metaBMA package.

text: second publication bias adjustment perform selection models. Selection models adjust different publication probabilities different p-value intervals. Selection models implemented weightr package (weightfunct() function; Coburn et al. (2019)) newly also metafor package (selmodel() function; Wolfgang (2010)). First, use weightr implementation fit “4PSM” selection model specifies three distinct p-value intervals: (1) covering range significant p-values effect sizes expected direction (0.00-0.025), (2) covering range “marginally” significant p-values effect sizes expected direction (0.025-0.05), (3) covering range non-significant p-values (0.05-1). use Cohen’s d transformation correlation coefficients since better maintaining distribution test statistics. fit model, need pass effect sizes (dfd$y) effect argument variances (dfd$se^2) v argument (note need pass vector values directly since weightfunct() function allow us pass data frame directly previous functions). set steps = c(0.025, 0.05) specify appropriate cut-points (note steps correspond one-sided p-values), set table = TRUE obtain frequency p values specified intervals. Note warning message informing us fact data contain sufficient number p-values one p-value intervals. model output obtained printing fitted model object fit_4PSM shows one p-value (0.025, 0.05) interval. can deal issue joining “marginally” significant non-significant p-value interval, resulting “3PSM” model. new model suffer estimation problem due limited number p-values intervals, can now interpret results confidence. First, check test heterogeneity clearly rejects null hypothesis Q(df = 17) = 75.4999, $p$ = 5.188348e-09 (find evidence heterogeneity, proceeded fitting fixed effects version model specifying fe = TRUE argument). follow checking test publication bias likelihood ratio test comparing unadjusted adjusted estimate X^2(df = 1) = 3.107176, $p$ = 0.077948. result test slightly ambiguous – reject null hypothesis publication bias α=0.10\alpha = 0.10 α=0.05\alpha = 0.05. decide interpret estimated effect size, transform back correlation scale. However, time need use d2r() function since supplied effect sizes Cohen’s d (note effect size estimate corresponds second value fit_3PSM$adj_est object random effect model, alternatively, simply use d2r(0.3219641)). text: third final publication bias adjustment perform robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA). RoBMA uses Bayesian model-averaging combine inference PET-PEESE selection models. use RoBMA R package (RoBMA() function; Bartoš & Maier (2020)) fit default 36 model ensemble (called RoBMA-PSMA) based orthogonal combination models assuming presence absence effect size, heterogeneity, publication bias. models assuming presence publication bias split six weight function models models utilizing PET PEESE publication bias adjustment. fit model, can directly pass original correlation coefficients r argument sample sizes n argument – RoBMA() function internally transform Fisher’s z scale , default, return estimates Cohen’s d scale used specify prior distributions (settings can changed prior_scale transformation arguments, output can conveniently transformed later). set model argument "PSMA" fit 36 model ensemble use seed argument make analysis reproducible (uses MCMC sampling contrast previous methods). turn parallel estimation setting parallel = TRUE argument (parallel processing might cases fail, try rerunning model one time turning parallel processing case). step can take time depending CPU. example, take approximately 1 minute fast CPU (e.g., AMD Ryzen 3900x 12c/24t) ten minutes longer slower CPUs (e.g., 2.7 GHz Intel Core i5). use summary() function explore details fitted model. printed output consists two parts. first table called Components summary contains information fitted models. tells us estimated ensemble 18/36 models assuming presence effect, 18/36 models assuming presence heterogeneity, 32/36 models assuming presence publication bias. second column summarizes prior model probabilities models assuming either presence individual components – , see presence absence components balanced priori. third column contains information posterior probability models assuming presence components – can observe posterior model probabilities models assuming presence effect slightly increased 0.552. last column contains information evidence favor presence components. Evidence presence effect undecided; models assuming presence effect 1.232 times likely given data models assuming absence effect. However, find overwhelming evidence favor heterogeneity, models assuming presence heterogeneity 19,168 times likely given data models assuming absence heterogeneity, moderate evidence favor publication bias. name indicates, second table called Model-averaged estimates contains information model-averaged estimates. first row labeled mu corresponds model-averaged effect size estimate (Cohen’s d scale) second row labeled tau corresponds model-averaged heterogeneity estimates. estimated model-averaged weights different p-value intervals PET PEESE regression coefficients. convert estimates correlation coefficients adding output_scale = "r" argument summary function. Now, obtained model-averaged effect size estimate correlation scale. interested estimates model-averaging across models assuming presence effect (effect size estimate), heterogeneity (heterogeneity estimate), publication bias (publication bias weights PET PEESE regression coefficients), added conditional = TRUE argument summary function. quick textual summary model can also generated interpret() function. can also obtain summary information individual models specifying type = "models" option. resulting table shows prior posterior model probabilities inclusion Bayes factors individual models (also set short_name = TRUE argument reducing width output abbreviating names prior distributions). obtain summary individual model diagnostics, set type = "diagnostics" argument. resulting table provides information maximum MCMC error, relative MCMC error, minimum ESS, maximum R-hat aggregating parameters model. can see, obtain acceptable ESS R-hat diagnostic values. Finally, can also plot model-averaged posterior distribution plot() function. set prior = TRUE argument include prior distribution grey line (arrow point density zero) output_scale = "r" transform posterior distribution correlation scale (default figure output Cohen’s d scale). text: RoBMA (Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis) R package estimating ensembles meta-analytic models using Bayesian model averaging. combines models /without effect, heterogeneity, publication bias, moderation, using Bayes factors component testing. text: function convenience wrapper around predict.brma(..., type = "effect", newdata = NULL). unweighted two-level normal models, true effects computed using empirical Bayes shrinkage: $$\theta_i = \lambda_i \cdot y_i + (1 - \lambda_i) \cdot \mu_i$$ \(\lambda_i = \tau^2 / (\tau^2 + se_i^2)\). likelihood weights, \(se_i^2\) replaced weighted sampling variance \(se_i^2 / w_i\). title: DFBETAS for brma Objects — dfbetas.brma
text: function computes DFBETAS values using Leave-One-(LOO) approximation based Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling (PSIS) weights. Ideally, DFBETAS defined : $$DFBETAS_{ij} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \hat{\beta}_{j(-)}}{SE(\hat{\beta}_{j(-)})}$$ \(\hat{\beta}_j\) estimate \(j\)-th coefficient using full data, \(\hat{\beta}_{j(-)}\) estimate observation \(\) omitted, \(SE(\hat{\beta}_{j(-)})\) standard error coefficient observation \(\) omitted. Bayesian context using LOO approximation: \(\hat{\beta}_{j(-)}\) estimated importance sampling weighted mean posterior samples, using PSIS weights \(w_{}\). \(SE(\hat{\beta}_{j(-)})\) estimated importance sampling weighted standard deviation posterior samples. approximation allows computing influence statistics without refitting model \(K\) times, making computationally efficient. type = "bias", fixed identification parameters (e.g., reference \(\omega = 1\) interval) can zero LOO posterior standard deviation. parameters retained output, DFBETAS values reported NaN standardized diagnostic undefined. Note: function requires LOO-CV computed model using add_loo.

title: Estimate Unit Information Standard Deviation — estimate_unit_information_sd
text: unit information standard deviation computed following Equation 6 Röver et al. (2021) : $$\text{UISD} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum n_i}{\sum \text{se}_i^{-2}}}$$ \(n_i\) sample size \(\text{se}_i\) standard error study. function useful want compute UISD pass multiple analyses via prior_unit_information_sd argument brma() related functions. ensures consistent prior scaling across analyses performed different subsets data.

title: Estimate Unit Information Standard Deviation — estimate_unit_information_sd
text: Röver C, Bender R, Dias S, Schmid CH, Schmidli H, Sturtz S, Weber S, Friede T (2021). “weakly informative prior distributions heterogeneity parameter Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis.” Research Synthesis Methods, 12(4), 448–474. doi:10.1002/jrsm.1475 .

text: Hat values (leverages) measure influence observation fitted values. Bayesian meta-analysis, random effects variance \(\tau^2\) uncertain, hat matrix depends posterior samples \(\tau^2\). function computes diagonal elements hat matrix: $$h_i = (X (X^T W X)^{-1} X^T W)_{ii}$$ \(W\) weight matrix inverse marginal variance matrix. hat matrix computed posterior draw averaged draws, matching vector output shape used metafor. method available normal outcome models without weightfunction selection.

title: Predict From brma Object — predict.brma
text: object fitted brma object newdata specification prediction data. Defaults NULL corresponds prediction observed data. Alternatives : TRUE returns single aggregated prediction (either scalar parameter models without moderators/scale, average across model matrix regression models). available type = "response" since observation-level sampling variance required. data.frame (meta-regression) named list effect size measure variability metrics (meta-analysis) new studies. input must contain variables used requested prediction type. Outcome columns optional type = "terms" unless PET/PEESE bias terms included via bias_adjusted = FALSE. type type prediction performed. Options : "terms" (alias: "marginal"): Fixed-effect parameters (mu). Produces mean effect size estimate given predictor levels, accounting random effects. "cluster": Fixed effects plus cluster-level random effects (mu + gamma). available multilevel (3-level) models. "estimate" (aliases: "effect", "blup"): True effects (mu + gamma + theta). existing normal data, returns posterior draws conditional BLUP means, simulated latent-effect draws. new data, samples estimate-level random effects. "response" (alias: "outcome"): Predicted observed values (yi). Incorporates heterogeneity sampling variability. "terms.scale": Scale parameter (tau), incorporating scale regression present. as_measure logical; whether convert GLMM response predictions simulated counts continuity-corrected effect-size estimators (logOR binomial, logIRR Poisson). Defaults TRUE. relevant GLMM models type = "response". FALSE, returns raw frequency data (counts). Use type = "estimate" latent logOR/logIRR predictions. output_measure effect-size measure location/effect predictions. Defaults fitted measure. title: Residuals for brma Objects — residuals.brma
text: object fitted brma object type type residuals compute. Options : "outcome" (default): Raw residuals (observed - fitted). Available model types. "pearson": Pearson (semi-standardized) residuals, dividing raw residuals marginal standard error \(\sqrt{v_i + \tau^2}\). available normal outcome models without selection (weightfunction) bias adjustment. "rstandard": Internally standardized residuals, dividing raw residuals standard errors computed using hat matrix. available normal outcome models without selection (weightfunction) bias adjustment. "LOO-PIT" (alias: "rstudent"): Leave-one-probability integral transform (PIT) residuals computed via Pareto smoothed importance sampling. LOO-CDF value observation computed transformed standard normal quantiles via \(\Phi^{-1}(u_i)\). correctly specified model, residuals follow standard normal distribution. recommended standardized residual Bayesian models properly accounts estimation uncertainty leverage. Available model types. Note: requires loo computed previously (see add_loo() function). unit output unit. "estimate" implemented currently.. conditioning_depth conditioning depth non-LOO residuals. "marginal" uses fixed effects , "cluster" conditions cluster-level random effects, "estimate" conditions full estimate-level fitted value. LOO-PIT residuals always use estimate-unit LOO target. bias_adjusted whether residuals computed bias-adjusted fitted values. Defaults FALSE, means residuals computed difference observed values raw (biased) predictions including PET/PEESE terms. Set TRUE compute residuals bias-corrected fitted values. Applies outcome Pearson residuals. Note bias-adjusted residuals residuals traditional sense. ... additional arguments.

title: Residuals for brma Objects — residuals.brma

title: Residuals for brma Objects — residuals.brma
text: Raw residuals (type = "outcome") computed : $$e_i = y_i - \hat{\mu}_i$$ \(y_i\) observed effect size \(\hat{\mu}_i\) fitted value (prediction fixed effects). Pearson residuals (type = "pearson") divide raw residuals marginal standard error: $$r_i^{Pearson} = \frac{e_i}{\sqrt{v_i + \tau^2}}$$ \(v_i\) sampling variance \(\tau^2\) relevant heterogeneity component. available normal outcome models without selection (weightfunction) bias adjustment. Standardized residuals (type = "rstandard") use hat matrix compute residual standard errors account uncertainty estimated coefficients: $$z_i = \frac{e_i}{\sqrt{[(-H)M(-H)']_{ii}}}$$ \(H\) hat matrix \(M\) marginal variance-covariance matrix. models without moderators, simplifies Pearson formula. available normal outcome models without selection (weightfunction) bias adjustment. LOO-PIT residuals (type = "LOO-PIT") Bayesian equivalent studentized deleted residuals (Vehtari et al. 2017) . computed via leave-one-probability integral transformation: $$r_i = \Phi^{-1}(u_i)$$ \(u_i = \sum_s w_{} F(y_i | \theta^{(s)})\) LOO-weighted CDF value, \(w_{}\) normalized PSIS weights, \(F\) cumulative distribution function estimate-unit predictive distribution used LOO. correctly specified model, LOO-PIT residuals follow standard normal distribution. Unlike traditional standardized residuals, LOO-PIT residuals properly account estimation uncertainty leverage without requiring hat matrix. recommended method standardized residuals Bayesian meta-analysis. meta-regression models, fitted values incorporate moderator effects. models without moderators, fitted values equal pooled effect. GLMM models (binomial Poisson), observed effect sizes sampling variances computed raw frequency data using formulas metafor::escalc default zero-cell adjustment (adding 0.5 cells cell zero). GLMM residuals LOO-PIT values therefore approximate effect-size-scale diagnostics, exact PIT diagnostics raw count likelihood. residuals computed separately posterior sample, naturally propagating uncertainty model parameters residuals.

title: Residuals for brma Objects — residuals.brma

what: The product space method for model-averaging
title: Prior specification for model-averaging — RoBMA_prior_specification
text: RoBMA implements Bayesian model-averaging using product space method (Carlin Chib 1995; Lodewyckx et al. 2011) . Rather fitting model separately combining results fitting complete, approach embeds competing models within single joint model space. discrete model indicator variable selects model component "active" MCMC iteration, posterior probability model estimated proportion iterations spent model's subspace. achieved specifying mixture priors combine: Null hypothesis component(s): Typically point masses (spikes) representing absence effect, heterogeneity, publication bias Alternative hypothesis component(s): Continuous distributions representing presence parameter mixture structure enables direct computation : Inclusion Bayes factors: Evidence presence vs. absence parameter (e.g., effect, heterogeneity, bias) Model-averaged estimates: Posterior estimates account model uncertainty weighting across models Conditional estimates: Posterior estimates given particular hypothesis true

Large absolute values may indicate outliers model misspecification. z column primary standardized diagnostic. resid se columns raw-scale companions computed LOO predictive moments using normalized PSIS weights. selection models, moments computed fitted selected-normal predictive distribution. GLMMs, computed approximate effect-size scale used LOO-PIT diagnostic; exact PIT diagnostics raw count likelihood. Unlike rstandard.brma (uses hat matrix), LOO-PIT residuals properly account estimation uncertainty leverage without requiring explicit hat matrix computation. makes rstudent.brma suitable model types including selection models GLMMs.

title: Externally Standardized (Studentized) Residuals for brma Objects — rstudent.brma

text: object class vif.brma containing: vif data frame columns term, df, GVIF, GVIF^(1/(2*df)) (= \(GVIF^{1/(2 \cdot df)}\)). single-df terms, GVIF equals standard VIF. posterior_correlation correlation matrix posterior regression coefficient samples requested available; otherwise NULL.

title: Variance Inflation Factors for brma Objects — vif.brma
text: VIF computed correlation matrix derived coefficient variance-covariance matrix \((X'WX)^{-1}\). standard meta-regression models, \(W = \mathrm{diag}(w_i/(v_i + \hat\tau^2))\) \(\hat\tau\) equal posterior mean heterogeneity. scale multilevel models, coefficient covariance averaged across posterior heterogeneity draws, using observation-specific \(\tau_i\) block-structured multilevel covariance applicable. VIF 1 indicates collinearity; values 5 10 commonly considered problematic. multi-column terms, factor contrasts, Generalized VIF (GVIF) Fox Monette (1992)  reported. GVIF captures joint inflation coefficients belonging term. enable comparison across terms different degrees freedom, \(GVIF^{1/(2 \cdot df)}\) also reported; value can compared usual VIF thresholds (squaring). posterior_correlation = TRUE, function also returns posterior correlation matrix regression coefficients. Bayesian diagnostic complements VIF: VIF diagnoses potential collinearity problems (data property), posterior correlation shows realized identification given data priors. Informative priors can mitigate collinearity, reducing posterior correlations even VIF high.

title: Variance Inflation Factors for brma Objects — vif.brma
text: Fox J, Monette G (1992). “Generalized collinearity diagnostics.” Journal American Statistical Association, 87(417), 178–183. doi:10.1080/01621459.1992.10475190 .
